public_rationale: The categorical denial of any measurable productivity benefit is contradicted under the stated reading. An [original study](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.01904v2) measures higher engineering output associated with LLM-tool adoption in April 2026 and checks several alternative explanations. This establishes a measurable benefit on an ordinary output-per-worker indicator, with substantial qualifications. It does not establish positive financial ROI, universal benefits or fulfillment of unspecified promises. Because the result depends on accepting that productivity indicator, interpretation_determines_result is true.
limitations: The decisive evidence is a preprint with nonrandom adoption.
Engineering output is a partial productivity measure; downstream costs and long-term quality remain incompletely measured.
The contradiction applies to the categorical productivity denial. The ROI and unspecified-promises clauses remain unsettled.

criteria.support_condition: Credible, sufficiently broad measurements for the target period establish no positive productivity or net financial returns from LLM use, and evaluations of identifiable maker promises establish their failure. Isolated unsuccessful deployments are insufficient to establish the categorical denial.
criteria.contradiction_condition: At least one credible comparison for the target period measures a positive productivity benefit attributable to LLM use, or a positive financial return after relevant costs. This contradicts the categorical benefits clause without establishing that all promises were fulfilled.

evidence.explanation: The study reports higher pull-request output per developer in April 2026 and a preferred estimate of 1.46 times output associated with adoption and accumulated use, after calendar-month controls. Checks address extra working days and splitting work, but nonrandom adoption, review burdens and incomplete quality measures limit causal certainty and prevent treating the result as financial ROI.

evidence.explanation: A randomized experiment found slower completion among experienced developers working in familiar repositories. This is material evidence that benefits vary by setting, but its February–June 2025 observations cannot establish the state of productivity in the target quarter.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Independent replication measuring working hours, useful completed work, downstream maintenance and all relevant costs would strengthen the assessment. Identifying the maker promises would allow that clause to be assessed separately.
